articles.title: Irmãos morrem afogados em RO ao rever família após 40 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Edio e Sebastião de Souza, de 68 e 69 anos, moravam em São Paulo. Segundo testemunhas, um deles passou mal na água e foi levado pela correnteza; o outro tentou ajudar e também se afogou.
articles.summary: Edio e Sebastião, de 68 e 69 anos, moravam em São Paulo. Segundo testemunhas, um deles passou mal na água e foi levado pela correnteza; o outro tentou ajudar e também se afogar.
articles.body:
Rio Jamari em Rondônia — Foto: Corpo de Bombeiros Militar de Rondônia

Dois irmãos morreram afogados no Rio Jamari, em Ariquemes (RO), na quarta-feira (16). Edio de Souza, de 68 anos, e Sebastião de Souza, de 69, moravam em São Paulo (SP) e viajavam por Rondônia para visitar parentes que não viam há 40 anos.

Segundo testemunhas, um dos homens passou mal e foi levado pela correnteza para uma área mais funda do rio. O outro tentou resgatá-lo, mas também se afogou. Exames periciais devem ser realizados para confirmar as causas das mortes.

O Corpo de Bombeiros foi acionado e iniciou as buscas ainda na tarde de quarta-feira, com o apoio de mergulhadores especializados. O corpo de Sebastião foi resgatado pelos socorristas por volta das 17h30 do mesmo dia. Já Edio foi localizado na manhã desta quinta-feira (17).

A família estava reunida para celebrar o reencontro. Enquanto Sebastião já havia visitado Rondônia anteriormente e mantinha contato com parentes locais, Edio viajou ao estado para rever o restante da família após décadas de distanciamento.

"Eles vieram para passar um momento de lazer. Estavam na prainha, perto da ilha, apenas brincando na beira do rio com o cachorro. Não faziam nenhuma atividade de risco quando a tragédia aconteceu", relatou um familiar.

articles.title: Couple bought a £1.2 million home with a dog-proof fence; years later, neighbours claimed half an acre of their garden
articles.summary: Rest of World News: David Todd and Caroline Hodge bought their £1.2 million home in East Sussex with a countryside setting and a secure fence that was important because t.
articles.body: David Todd and Caroline Hodge bought their £1.2 million home in East Sussex with a countryside setting and a secure fence that was important because they owned two Labradors. Years later, however, that same fence became the centre of a dispute with their new neighbours. The disagreement focused on about half an acre of land that Todd and Hodge believed was part of their garden. Their neighbours argued that the land belonged to them, based on the legal boundary recorded for the property.The £1.2 million home and its disputed dog-proof fence According to The Independent, David Todd, 69, and Caroline Hodge, 65, bought Wyland Wood near Robertsbridge, East Sussex, for around £1.2 million in 2018. This 19th-century detached stone house has four bedrooms and three bathrooms and sits within 2.7 acres of gardens and woodland. It also has a drawing room, a dog and boot room and a treehouse.The couple had particular reason to value the fencing around the property. The Independent reported that estate agents had assured the couple that the garden was enclosed by a dog-proof fence, something they considered important because they owned two Labradors. Hodge described the dogs as their sweethearts during the earlier court proceedings.At the time they bought the property, the fence was already in place and appeared to provide a clear physical edge around the garden. The couple later argued that they reasonably believed everything inside it was part of the property they were purchasing.The situation changed after Richard Marsh, 44, and his wife Rebecca, 40, bought neighbouring ancient woodland and an adjoining meadow in May 2021, as reported by The Independent.What changed after the Marshes bought the neighbouring landThe disagreement began when the Marshes determined that the existing fence did not match the boundary shown in the Land Registry records. They maintained that about half an acre inside the fence actually belonged to them, along with an important strip providing access to their land.The Independent reported that Marsh then began removing sections of the existing fence and intended to put up a new one along the boundary shown on the property documents. Todd and Hodge objected, saying this would take part of what they understood to be their garden.The couple obtained a court injunction requiring Marsh to stop removing the fence, preventing him from putting up a replacement and requiring sections that had already been removed to be restored.The disagreement eventually reached court, where the question was not simply where the visible fence stood, but which line legally represented the boundary between the two properties.How did the courts determine where the boundary layAt the 2025 county court hearing, Judge Caroline Parker ruled in favour of the Marshes. According to The Independent, she found that sections of the dog-proof fence stood between 6 and 8 metres outside the paper boundary of the land.That boundary was identified by a tree line and remnants of an older wire fence. The judge accepted that Todd and Hodge believed the existing fence marked the edge of their garden and noted that it was more obvious on the ground than the tree line.However, the court decided that describing the garden as dog-proof in the estate agent’s particulars was not enough to establish that the fence represented the legal boundary.The judge also ruled that the disputed half acre could be fenced off by the Marshes. They were awarded £3,174 in damages. The ruling meant that the couple lost a sizable section of the garden they had believed came with Wyland Wood.The couple challenged the original ruling based on the previous ownerTodd and Hodge appealed the decision, arguing that a reasonable purchaser would have understood the visible fence to mark the property's boundary.They also relied on a separate argument involving the previous owner of the Marshes’ land, Stephen Baldwin. The couple said emails exchanged with Baldwin while discussing repairs to the fence, amounted to a boundary agreement. Their position was that the correspondence showed the land inside the fence belonged to Wyland Wood.According to The Independent, Todd’s barrister argued that a boundary agreement could arise even without a formal dispute about the boundary. The couple’s case was that the existing fence had been treated as the boundary during discussions about repairing it.The Marshes rejected that interpretation. Their barrister argued that the emails were about sharing repair costs rather than agreeing where the property boundary stood.What did the High Court decide about the half acreIn July 2026, the High Court dismissed Todd and Hodge’s appeal, according to The Independent. Mr Justice Michael Green upheld the earlier decision that the legal boundary was the one shown on the registered title plans and historical property documents, rather than the dog-proof fence.The court noted that the fence ran parallel to the paper boundary but stood between 6.37 metres and 11.37 metres on the Marshes’ side of it.The judge also rejected the claim that the emails with Baldwin created a boundary agreement. The discussions had concerned repairs to the fence, rather than its precise legal position. The court found that Baldwin had not consciously considered the boundary when agreeing to share repair costs.As a result, the long-running dispute ended with the paper boundary remaining in place. The fence that had helped Todd and Hodge feel their dogs and garden were secure could not be treated as the legal dividing line between the properties.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Houthi drone debris kills one, injures two in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Middle East News: Saudi Arabia said on Thursday that debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed one person and injured two others in Taif, as fighting between the I.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia said on Thursday that debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed one person and injured two others in Taif, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group, Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and their allies intensified amid the wider Middle East conflict.Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence said the falling debris caused “one death, two injuries, and material damage to several buildings and vehicles”. The person killed was a Yemeni national, while the injured included a Saudi citizen and a Pakistani resident, according to Saudi authorities.The incident came a day after Riyadh said it had intercepted a drone headed towards Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca, while Iran’s Foreign Ministry urged against using claims over drone interceptions to escalate tensions.The renewed violence follows the collapse of a fragile truce in Yemen and a fresh Houthi offensive that has seen the group make gains along the Red Sea coast. Reuters reported that thousands of Yemenis were fleeing by sea as fighting intensified, with more than 100,000 people displaced by the renewed conflict.The strategic stakes have also widened beyond Yemen. The Houthis have taken control of areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s key maritime chokepoints, raising concerns over shipping and energy supplies. Reuters said the group’s gains had increased risks around a route critical to global trade.On Thursday, the Houthi-backed Almasirah television reported that Saudi warplanes had struck telecommunications towers in Taiz province, killing one civilian and injuring another. It also reported that three children were killed in strikes by forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government. Those claims could not be independently verified.Saudi Arabia’s latest casualties have also placed renewed attention on its defence arrangements with Pakistan and Turkiye. The three countries recently signed a defence pact, while Pakistan has said the agreement could become operational in the event of aggression against Saudi Arabia.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: RANDOM MUSING | DIVIDED KINGDOM? Why Scotland, Wales and Ireland want to 'leave' the UK
articles.summary: UK News: Explore the growing movements in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland for independence from the UK, spurred by Brexit and recent political statements from Donald Trump. What does this mean for the future of the United Kingdom?
articles.body: The Partition of India — and before it the Partition of Bengal — were among the most consequential acts of British imperial cartography, with the former leaving countless dead, a subcontinent in perennial trauma and perhaps even helping create some of the geopolitical conditions from which pan-global Islamist terrorism later emerged with a little help from Uncle Sam. Ergo, there is a little schadenfreude in seeing talk of partition engulf the country that facilitated it: the United Kingdom, or should we call it the Divided Kingdom?The latest shot comes from the person whose logorrhoea has truly upended the world order carefully put in place after the Second World War. Speaking in Ireland, Donald Trump put the fat in the fire by saying he would “love” to see a “united” Ireland, saying it was inevitable and “may as well happen now”. UK PM Andy Burnham – who, if you squint your eye, looks like an AI-generated image of Keir Starmer – pushed back, only for Trump to double down and call it “pretty cool”.Now, for Trump, saying something is “pretty cool” could be as serious as toppling a Supreme Leader or having regular Coke instead of Diet Coke, but his statement certainly caused some excitement.Now here’s the reason why Trump’s rhetoric is a little more than just words.For perhaps the first time in their history, Ireland, Scotland and Wales are led by parties and politicians who want to change their nations’ relationship with the UK, a sort of Brexit, if you will, except this was never how Brexit was supposed to work.The Brexit Referendum in 2016, which is as hackneyed as Yes Minister’s British sausage plot to get Jim Hacker elected as PM, has consumed six Prime Ministers, effectively turning 10 Downing Street into an AirBNB.Instead of freeing the UK from the bureaucrats in Brussels, it has instead put a man who recently beat a novelty candidate wearing a trash can within touching distance of the Prime Minister’s seat. And now it has created a political situation where the UK might finally become “divided”. Britain has survived the Spanish Armada, Napoleon, two world wars, the loss of empire, the Troubles, Brexit and even Meghan Markle — but it might not survive Donald Trump.Scotland wants independence, Plaid Cymru (Wales’ governing party) is toying with the idea, and Sinn Fein wants Northern Ireland to leave one state and join another.In Ted Lasso, the Panglossian protagonist once asked: “How many countries are in this country?” And to explain that properly, we have to go back to the World Cup quarter-final when England faced Erling Haaland and Norway. In a way, Haaland’s predecessors, the Vikings, are responsible for what we call the United Kingdom. Unlike Haaland and his compatriots, who weren’t that successful while raiding the English defence, his predecessors attacked so much that the warring Anglo-Saxon tribes had to band together under Alfred the Great before Æthelstan put together what can be recognised as the first united England.Once it had set its own affairs in order, England turned to its neighbours, conquering Wales. The neighbour that gave the most trouble — and not just because of Mel Gibson’s antisemitic views — was Scotland, which continued to resist England.Edward I tried, William Wallace resisted, Robert the Bruce won at Bannockburn in the first Spiderman prequel and Scotland remained sovereign. And then in 1603 the joke wrote itself when James VI of Scotland inherited England. No invasion was needed, but the two kingdoms retained separate parliaments and laws, perhaps because the Scots were always wary of the English.That arrangement spectacularly imploded under James’s son Charles I, whose quarrels with Parliament eventually produced civil wars across England, Scotland and Ireland and ended with the rather permanent constitutional remedy of chopping off the king’s head. Ireland was already deeply entangled in the mess after the rebellion of 1641, and when Oliver Cromwell crossed the Irish Sea in 1649, he ended up causing far more damage than the Dothraki and the Unsullied did on Westeros.Abolishing the monarchy, Lord-Protector Cromwell briefly pulled England, Scotland and Ireland into one republican experiment which was as successful as the MAGA Republican experiment. Cromwell’s Puritan regime was so maudlin that the entire kingdom decided that it was considerably less irritating to have a Crown than a prude in charge.While the monarchy returned with Charles II, the constitutional problem remained as all three countries continued to behave on their own. The marriage between England and Scotland began properly in 1707 because England wanted a common Protestant succession and Scotland’s elite wanted to dip their fingers into the giant and ever-expanding pie that was the English colonial markets. The Acts of Union created Great Britain, and Scots subsequently became energetic participants in the British Empire.Ireland, however, kind of like Roy Keane in his last days at Manchester United, continued to rage. It had been under varying degrees of English control for centuries, beginning with the Anglo-Norman invasion, through the Tudor conquest and Cromwell’s campaigns. It still remained a separate kingdom, and after the 1798 rebellion and with the French making eyes, London decided enough was enough. While the Irish Commons initially rejected the offer, palms were greased with peerages, pensions and patronage to create the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.Like Roy Keane at Manchester United after his epic MUTV rant, the arrangement didn’t last, with Irish nationalism, the Easter Rising and the War of Independence eventually producing the Anglo-Irish Treaty, and in 1922 most of Ireland chose Brexit while Northern Ireland remained.As the empire crumbled under its own guilt, Westminster tried devolution, with the Scots getting a parliament, Wales an assembly and the Good Friday Agreement creating power-sharing in Northern Ireland in an awkward situationship in which, if a majority of Northern Ireland wanted it, it could become a part of a united Ireland.And things roiled on, despite the fireworks brought by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) – seldom referred to as terrorists because they are white – ending with the aforementioned Good Friday Agreement in 1998. IRA’s political wing Sinn Fein was admitted into the multi-party peace talks and by 2005 the IRA put down its arms, realising there were better ways to make noise.And then came Brexit, in which Scotland voted heavily to Remain, Northern Ireland voted Remain, while Wales voted Leave alongside England.Now Scotland has the most mature independence movement, with the SNP holding 58 and the pro-independence Greens 15, giving them 73 in a 129-seat assembly.While Scotland has a fair degree of freedom with its own parliament and legal system, foreign affairs, immigration and monetary policy are still decided in Westminster. Now Scottish independence enthusiasts argue that leaving the UK would allow Scotland to pull off its own reverse Brexit and rejoin the EU, which would be better for Scottish economic policy and allow it to have its own affairs.Meanwhile, the unionists – those who want things to remain as they are – and who, funnily enough, are the most hardcore Trump supporters, argue that the fiscal deficit would make it difficult, and with independence would come arguments about tax, spending, debt, and basically that adulting will be too expensive, something every youngster learns once they leave their parents’ house.Wales, on the other hand, the least insouciant of the English neighbours, has Plaid Cymru in charge. The desire for independence is less than Scottish levels, and while it has ruled out a referendum, it argues that Wales could have a whale of a time if it possessed a little more freedom.And Northern Ireland’s break for freedom is more Winky than Dobby, because Sinn Fein isn’t proposing a new country: it just wants reunification with an existing EU member state.Of course, none of this could have happened without Brexit, which, with the benefit of hindsight, tells us that one shouldn’t leave the fate of a nation to overgrown public schoolboys who have to remain tight-lipped about hogs to call referendums that really aren’t needed. Despite a majority after many years of torrid Tory misrule, Labour is hurtling from one disaster to another and looks set to say ‘fare thee well’ if an election was held. But perhaps the biggest irony was Nigel Farage, Donald Trump’s most beloved British politician, who loves crypto as much as his special friend, having to break from his MAGA buddy to insist that Northern Ireland will remain an integral part of the UK.The irony is quite delicious because Great Britain has spent many centuries drawing borders, joining kingdoms, partitioning countries and deciding what flag will flutter over people’s heads. At one time it had an empire so vast that the sun didn’t set on it. Whether the United Kingdom becomes divided is ultimately for the people living in its constituent nations to decide – a right that many who were ruled by Great Britain never had – but for those of us who lived under the yoke of colonial rule, there’s a certain historical irony in watching Britain discover it’s considerably less fun when someone draws and redraws borders based on their own fancies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Two Washington entrepreneurs started a dog-waste cleanup business with about $1,000; six years later, Swoop Scoop says the operation generates more than $200,000 a month across multiple markets
articles.summary: US News: What started as a small Washington business built around one of the least glamorous chores of dog ownership has grown into a multi-market operation ge.
articles.body: What started as a small Washington business built around one of the least glamorous chores of dog ownership has grown into a multi-market operation generating more than $200,000 a month. William Milliken and Levi Swartz founded Swoop Scoop in late 2020 in Spokane Valley, Washington, after recognising that picking up dog waste was an overlooked service that many pet owners would gladly outsource. According to the episode of Millionaire University, featuring Swoop Scoop president Milliken, the entrepreneurs started the business with about $1,000 and grew it from roughly 20 customers to more than 300 within just a few months. In the episode, Milliken says the company now generates more than $200,000 a month and has expanded into multiple markets. Swoop Scoop's own website describes the company as a dog-waste removal service created to make life easier for pet owners and says it now serves customers across multiple markets.From a simple chore to a business ideaThe concept behind Swoop Scoop was straightforward. Milliken and Swartz had both spent years cleaning up after their own dogs and recognised an opportunity in a chore that was necessary but rarely enjoyable. Rather than creating a new product, the founders focused on providing a service. Customers could pay someone else to regularly remove dog waste from their yards, turning an unpleasant household task into a recurring business relationship.According to Swoop Scoop, the company was founded in late 2020 in Spokane Valley with the goal of eliminating what it describes as one of the most dreaded chores for dog owners. The company says its founders recognised that professional pooper-scooping was an overlooked service across the United States. That basic idea became the foundation for a business that could grow one customer and one neighbourhood at a time.Starting with about $1,000The company's beginnings were modest. Milliken told Millionaire University that he and Swartz started Swoop Scoop with about $1,000. The business then grew rapidly, with the podcast reporting that its customer base expanded from roughly 20 customers to more than 300 in a matter of months. The founders used relatively straightforward marketing methods to attract customers. Milliken discusses Facebook advertising in the podcast, along with the importance of recurring subscription revenue to the company's model.That recurring element is particularly important for a service such as dog-waste removal. A customer who signs up for regular cleaning can generate repeated revenue rather than providing the company with only a single transaction. The podcast describes this as part of the appeal of so-called “boring” businesses, where a simple service can create a dependable customer relationship without requiring a large initial investment.Why dog-waste removal can scaleDog-waste removal may not sound like a conventional high-growth business, but its simplicity can also make the model relatively easy to replicate. A worker does not need to manufacture a product or maintain a large inventory. The company instead organises routes, schedules recurring visits and provides the service at customers' homes.Swoop Scoop's current website shows how the original idea has developed into a broader service business. The company says it provides dog-waste removal and has built a team focused on delivering what it describes as a professional, “white glove” experience for customers. The company has also expanded geographically. Its website lists service areas including Spokane, Seattle, Everett and North Idaho, reflecting its growth beyond the Spokane Valley market where it began.Expanding beyond SpokaneThe expansion accelerated as Swoop Scoop built its customer base and operations. In 2023, the company, then known as Scoop Troop, acquired Dooky's Pet Waste Removal for $54,000, according to the Spokane Journal of Business. At the time, the company had more than 1,500 customers and about a dozen employees and had expanded into Seattle.The company subsequently operated under the Swoop Scoop name as it continued developing its brand and expanding its reach. The company's growth has also been reflected outside its own reporting. Swoop Scoop was included on the 2025 Inc. 5000 list at No. 653, with Inc. reporting 638% three-year growth. A Spokane Journal of Business report on the Inc. 5000 recognition said the company's revenue had increased 638% between 2021 and 2024. It also reported that Swoop Scoop had locations in Seattle and Everett, Washington, and North Idaho.Building around recurring customersThe subscription model remains central to the company's approach. Instead of waiting for customers to call whenever their yards need cleaning, recurring services allow the company to schedule regular visits. That creates a predictable need for the customer and a repeat service opportunity for the business. The Millionaire University episode specifically identifies recurring subscription revenue as one of the reasons the business model is attractive. The podcast also discusses seasonal demand, expanding into new markets and knowing when to pivot as part of the challenges involved in growing the company.For Swoop Scoop, scaling therefore involves more than simply finding more people willing to scoop dog waste. It requires building routes, hiring and managing workers, maintaining customer relationships and entering new markets while keeping the service consistent.More than a dog-waste businessThe company's services have expanded beyond routine residential cleanups. Swoop Scoop's website describes its broader offering as including residential and commercial pet-waste removal, along with odour-control services. The company has also developed expertise around the business itself. Its broader ecosystem includes resources aimed at people interested in starting or growing businesses in the pet-waste-removal industry. That reflects how a service that began as a small local operation has evolved into a business model that the founders believe can be replicated in other markets.From $1,000 to more than $200,000 a monthThe numbers now associated with Swoop Scoop are far removed from its beginnings. The Millionaire University episode describes the company as a multi-million-dollar operation generating more than $200,000 every month. It also highlights the jump from roughly 20 customers to more than 300 within a few months and the company's expansion into multiple markets. Meanwhile, the company's own website documents its origins, its expansion into multiple markets and its focus on making dog ownership easier by taking over the task of waste removal.The Swoop Scoop story illustrates how a business does not necessarily need an elaborate product or a huge starting investment to find a market. Two entrepreneurs began with about $1,000 and a service built around a chore many people would rather avoid. Six years later, their company says it has grown into a multi-market operation generating more than $200,000 a month, turning an ordinary household nuisance into the foundation of a sizeable business.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Elon Musk's mother Maye Musk said Elon always wanted to do good for others even when he was a child, but his approach often put him at odds with others. Maye opened up about her personal journey in an interview with CBS Mornings co-host Gayle King on her new memoir "Timeless". Maye said Elon Musk was a genius child and he ""just wants to do good in the world, but that means you stand on a lot of toes." She said she believes he's been treated unfairly by members of the public."People are mean. And they're strangers, or they're not accomplished themselves, and then they can do insults," she said. "It makes me angry."She said she wants people to know, "He does whatever is best for America and what's best for the world," adding, "And then, if we don't listen, then let's go to Mars."Her comments come after a turbulent period for Elon Musk, whose brief stint in the US government as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, drew considerable criticism. DOGE overhauled federal agencies and cut funding for several programmes during the early months of President Donald Trump’s second term.Musk later had a public falling-out with Trump after leaving the administration, including criticism of Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill”. The relationship has since appeared to improve. Musk has also backed Republican candidates in the 2026 midterm elections. Meanwhile, his business empire has continued to expand. SpaceX went public, making Musk the world's first trillionaire.When Gayle King asked Maye Musk whether she agreed that Elon was on the spectrum as a child, Maye said: "Well, when I read 'the spectrum,' maybe on one of the points that he's a little awkward, yeah."In her memoir, Maye recounted her struggle in an abusive marriage and how she moved from South Africa to Canada with her three children, where she started her own practice as a dietitian. "I didn't know it was possible," she said. "Until you just have enough, and you run away."Maye said her children did not complain when she was juggling parenting and her studies for her first master's degree and when they all had to sleep on couches and floors. "I said to them, 'Why did you put up with that?' And they said, 'Well, if we complained, would you listen?' And I said 'No,'" Musk recalled.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Anna’s hummingbirds were absent from Portland before 1968, but today they are among the city’s most common birds after expanding north
articles.summary: US News: Anna’s hummingbirds have expanded their range across the Pacific Northwest, with a presence in cities such as Portland, Oregon. Once largely associate.
articles.body: Anna’s hummingbirds have expanded their range across the Pacific Northwest, with a presence in cities such as Portland, Oregon. Once largely associated with California, the small, colourful birds gradually moved north and established populations in Oregon, Washington and British Columbia. Records show that numbers remained low for decades before rising rapidly from the late 1990s. Today, Portland has an estimated abundance of 2.01 Anna’s hummingbirds per party-hour, placing it alongside cities in northern California. Researchers link the expansion to population growth, introduced plants, ornamental gardens and hummingbird feeders, while climate change may have helped the species colonise some colder areas.Portland’s Anna’s hummingbirds took decades to spreadAccording to the study published in The University of Chicago Press, titled ‘Ecological Release of the Anna’s Hummingbird during a Northern Range Expansion’, the history of Anna’s hummingbirds in the Pacific Northwest is therefore not simply a story of birds arriving and immediately becoming abundant. The research found that populations in Oregon, Washington and British Columbia were present by the early 1970s, but they remained at low densities for decades. In the north-west, populations were consistently recorded from the mid-1960s, followed by a much faster rise from the late 1990s.Portland provides a striking example of how far that change went. In the study’s abundance estimates, Portland recorded 2.01 birds per party-hour, compared with 1.74 in Seattle, 1.92 in Oakland and 1.89 in San Jose. In other words, the Portland figure had reached levels comparable with cities in the northern part of the hummingbird’s historic range. The research also notes that populations in the Pacific Northwest show stronger growth than those in the species’ native range.Eucalyptus helped Anna’s hummingbirds expandEarlier increases in Anna’s hummingbird numbers in California were associated with the spread of introduced flowering plants, particularly eucalyptus. The trees provided nectar during periods when food could otherwise become scarce. Historical accounts cited by the study suggested that this helped support larger wintering populations.The research describes how hummingbird feeders and ornamental garden plants helped support newly established populations in areas where the species had previously been uncommon. A separate study cited by Battey found that Anna’s hummingbirds in their expanded northern range were more likely to visit feeders and use human-modified landscapes. The relationship could also reinforce itself: people who noticed hummingbirds were more likely to put up feeders, potentially increasing the food available to the birds.Climate change may have supported Northern ExpansionClimate change may have helped the birds colonise some northern locations, but the study does not identify it as the main explanation for the earliest stages of the expansion. Climate models based on conditions from 1895–1925 failed to predict the newly occupied areas of the Pacific Northwest. However, the researchers found that the area with minimum breeding-season temperatures suitable for the species increased by about 11% between 1895–1925 and 1995–2015.The birds have also adjusted their breeding schedule as they moved north. Nest records showed that the median nesting date in the Pacific Northwest was 11 days later than in California, while the beginning of the nesting season shifted by roughly 17–32 days in the comparison. The study concludes that Anna’s hummingbirds have become common breeding birds across the lowland Pacific Northwest by combining range expansion, changes in nesting timing and increasing use of human-modified habitats.Portland’s estimated abundance had reached 2.01 birds per party-hour, showing how a bird that was once unusual in the region had become a familiar part of the city’s birdlife.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US News: The FBI warned that a small group of women allegedly created fake online dating profiles using a “traditional wife” or “tradwife” image to attract US .
articles.body: The FBI warned that a small group of women allegedly created fake online dating profiles using a “traditional wife” or “tradwife” image to attract US immigration enforcement officers and expose their personal information online.The FBI’s Chicago office circulated a memo to law enforcement agencies in February about the alleged tactic, The Guardian reported, citing a document obtained through a public records request by government transparency nonprofit Property of the People.The memo said the women were allegedly creating fictitious dating profiles to attract and then “dox” law enforcement personnel involved in immigration enforcement.Fake profiles designed to attract officersAccording to the FBI briefing, the profiles used “traditional wife” imagery and listed specific interests intended to appeal to law enforcement personnel. The alleged objective was to lure officers into online or in-person interactions under the guise of a date and then publicly expose their identities and personal information.The FBI said the tactic was intended to cause public embarrassment and discourage immigration enforcement activity.However, the briefing did not identify the dating platforms allegedly used, specify where the women were based, or say whether any immigration officers had actually been exposed. The FBI also described the document as “not finally evaluated intelligence” and said it was issued to raise awareness about the alleged doxing technique.Property of the People obtained the memo through a public records request. The FBI memo came weeks after a New York Post report claimed that social media users were encouraging women to use dating apps to identify and expose ICE agents.That report cited posts from conservative account Libs of TikTok, but did not provide evidence that agents had actually been tricked.Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, criticised the FBI briefing, calling it a thinly sourced alert over alleged online dating attempts involving ICE agents.The FBI has issued other internal warnings about the doxing of immigration enforcement personnel. articles.title: No official dinners, foreign travel: Pakistan rolls out austerity measures amid fuel shock
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan on Thursday announced a fresh set of austerity measures, including a 50 per cent cut in fuel allocations for government vehicles and a ban on.
articles.body: Pakistan on Thursday announced a fresh set of austerity measures, including a 50 per cent cut in fuel allocations for government vehicles and a ban on official foreign travel and the purchase of new government vehicles. The measures come as rising global oil prices threaten fuel, gas and power supplies.The measures, approved by the Pakistan cabinet, will remain in force for three months as the government seeks to reduce fuel consumption and public expenditure.Under the new restrictions, markets will have to close by 9 pm, while marriage halls can operate until 10 pm and restaurants until 11 pm. Drug stores and medical laboratories have been exempted.Fuel allocations for government vehicles will be reduced by half, although vehicles used by the armed forces, law enforcement agencies and essential services will not be covered by the cut.The Shehbaz Sharif government has also ordered a five per cent reduction in non-employee-related expenditure and prohibited official foreign visits and domestic travel for meetings, directing officials to use virtual meetings instead.Official dinners have been banned, except those hosted for foreign visitors and delegations. The purchase of new government vehicles has also been prohibited, while procurement of durable goods has been restricted, with IT purchases exempted.The measures come two days after Pakistan raised petrol prices by PkR 4.10 per litre and high-speed diesel (HSD) by PkR 6.41 per litre. Petrol now costs PkR 384.34 per litre, while HSD is priced at PkR 415.83.Global oil prices have risen amid continuing conflict and supply concerns in West Asia, including attacks on energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the temporary closure of its East-West oil pipeline following an aerial attack.The austerity package is the second such effort this year. Pakistan introduced similar measures in March, including a temporary school shutdown, reductions in government fuel use and greater reliance on remote working.Earlier the government had introduced the Prime Minister's Fuel Relief Scheme from Wednesday, offering motorcycle, rickshaw and small-car owners a subsidy of 100 rupees (36 US cents) per litre on a capped monthly quota.The programme, however, has faced implementation difficulties. Karachi resident Mohammad Musharraf told Reuters: "First of all, you have to register your vehicle. Then you have to register your mobile phone. How can an illiterate person survive if the conditions are so difficult?"The energy pressures extend beyond transport. Reuters reported that Pakistan's power sector could require up to 400 million cubic feet of gas a day through winter, while only two LNG cargoes had been confirmed for September.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1919, William Wrigley Jr. transformed Catalina Island into a tourist destination; 56 years later, his family put 88% of it under conservation
articles.summary: US News: For more than half a century, the Wrigley family helped shape the future of Catalina Island, first as a commercial investment and later as a conservat.
articles.body: For more than half a century, the Wrigley family helped shape the future of Catalina Island, first as a commercial investment and later as a conservation legacy. William Wrigley Jr., the chewing-gum businessman, became a major investor in the Santa Catalina Island Company in 1919 and helped expand tourism, infrastructure and attractions across the island. His family’s involvement continued after his death in 1932, eventually shifting towards protecting Catalina’s undeveloped landscapes. In 1972, the Catalina Island Conservancy was established. Three years later, the family transferred 42,135 acres to the organisation, placing roughly 88% of the island under its care.How William Wrigley Jr. built the fortune behind CatalinaWilliam Wrigley Jr. was born in Philadelphia in 1861 and had already built a considerable business empire before Catalina entered his life. His rise began in an unusual way. He initially sold his father's soap, using baking powder as an incentive for customers to buy it. When people showed greater interest in the free product, he changed direction.As reported by Love Catalina Island Tourism Authority, Chewing gum eventually became the centre of the business. Brands including Juicy Fruit, Spearmint and Doublemint helped turn the Wrigley name into a national one, while the company's advertising became a major part of its success.By the time Wrigley became involved with Catalina, he had the money and commercial experience to reshape the island on a much larger scale. The Santa Catalina Island Company had been established in the 1890s by the Banning brothers, who had developed the island as a resort. Wrigley became a major investor in 1919 and eventually gained controlling interest.Catalina was not simply a holiday destination waiting to be marketed, though. Its communities and infrastructure needed investment, and a major fire had devastated much of Avalon before Wrigley's period of ownership.How Wrigley turned Catalina into a major tourist destinationWrigley put money into roads, utilities, housing and attractions while also working to make the island more accessible to visitors. His approach combined the practical side of running a large property with the publicity methods that had already made his chewing gum company successful.According to the Catalina Island Company, the most recognisable result was the Catalina Casino, completed in 1929. The circular building became an enduring part of Avalon's waterfront and remains one of the island's best-known landmarks. Wrigley's influence also extended into sport. He had acquired an interest in the Chicago Cubs in 1916 and became the club's principal owner in 1921. That same year, the Cubs began holding spring training on Catalina, starting a relationship with the island that lasted for almost three decades.The baseball connection mattered beyond the games themselves. Players, journalists and baseball followers were introduced to Catalina, giving the island a national audience at a time when mass tourism and modern advertising were developing rapidly.According to Love Catalina Island Tourism Authority, Wrigley also worked with designers Dorothy and Otis Shepard on promotional material for Catalina. Advertising, sporting events and unusual attractions helped establish the island as a destination rather than simply another piece of coastal property.Catalina’s undeveloped landscape became a conservation priorityWilliam Wrigley Jr. died in 1932, but his connection with Catalina did not end there. His son, Philip Knight Wrigley, inherited an important role in the family's island interests and continued many of the projects his father had started.The family maintained its involvement through the Santa Catalina Island Company while Catalina went through several different phases, including the disruption caused by the Second World War. Tourism later returned, and the island continued developing as a resort while large areas remained outside the built-up centres.There was also a gradual change in the family's approach to the island's undeveloped interior. Protecting Catalina's landscape became a more formal objective rather than simply an aspect of managing the property. That shift eventually produced the Catalina Island Conservancy.A conservation organisation was created in 1972The Catalina Island Conservancy was established in 1972 with involvement from members of the Wrigley and Offield families. Its purpose was to provide a permanent organisation responsible for conserving and managing much of Catalina's natural land.The timing is important because the major land transfer did not actually occur in 1972. Three years later, the Wrigley family completed the step that changed the ownership of most of Catalina's interior.Before that happened, the Santa Catalina Island Company had already entered into an agreement with Los Angeles County in 1974 covering about 41,000 acres. The arrangement restricted development and provided for recreational and educational use while maintaining the area's open-space character. Then came the larger and more permanent transfer.A 1975 land transfer secured protection for 88% of Catalina IslandOn 15 February 1975, Philip K. Wrigley, his wife Helen and his sister Dorothy Wrigley Offield, acting through the Santa Catalina Island Company, deeded 42,135 acres of Santa Catalina Island to the Catalina Island Conservancy.The figure represents roughly 88% of the island. The transfer included most of Catalina's interior and a substantial stretch of coastline, giving the Conservancy responsibility for an enormous area of land outside the main resort communities.The 1975 conveyance became the key step in securing permanent protection for most of the island. The distinction between the two dates matters. The Conservancy was formed in 1972; the 42,135-acre transfer was completed in 1975.The transfer left Catalina with two very different rolesThe arrangement did not mean that every part of Catalina became a protected wilderness area with no tourism. The Santa Catalina Island Company retained land and continued operating much of the island's resort and visitor business, particularly in Avalon and Two Harbors. The Conservancy became responsible for the much larger area of wildland.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US secures release of detained citizen Adam Castillo in Myanmar
articles.summary: Businessman Adam Castillo had been detained by authorities for three months on breach of trust allegations.
articles.body:
The United States State Department has helped to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen detained in Myanmar for three months.

A delegation of US officials travelled to ⁠Myanmar’s capital, Naypyidaw, last week to speak with local officials about his case, the State Department said on Thursday.

Myanmar state media reported that Castillo, 40, was flown out of the capital “in consideration of the friendly relations between Myanmar and the United States”. State media said he had been charged with breach of trust allegations, and that he had violated the regulations of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, a business group for which he served as president.

Castillo was released into the custody of US officials and then flew to Bangkok, Thailand.

“We are thrilled to see Adam coming home and are grateful for the collaboration and efforts from the Trump administration,” said Mickey Bergman, CEO of Global Reach, a Washington-based nonprofit that helped Castillo’s family advocate for his release, referring to US President Donald Trump.

“I can’t wait to welcome my brother home, but I know it will be bittersweet for him,” said his sister Amanda Castillo in a statement. “He had such great hopes for enhanced US/Myanmar relations, and he holds the deepest respect for the Burmese people, among whom he lived for many years.”

The former US Marine, who was a founder and owner of the security risk management firm AGS Myanmar, was detained at Yangon International Airport on June 11 after returning from Malaysia.

The arrest came after the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar accused him of financial impropriety, which he denies. At the time, Myanmar authorities would only say he had been arrested because “there was a crime and a lawsuit”, but did not provide further details.

articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Thursday said the United States was making progress towards establishing a permanent Army base in Poland, signalling a potentially significant expansion of the American military presence on NATO’s eastern flank.Trump attributed the progress to what he called the “bold leadership” of Polish President Karol Nawrocki. In a post on Truth Social, he said the location of the proposed base could be announced soon. "GREAT NEWS! Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a U.S. Army base in Poland," Trump posted.“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance,” he added.Poland has sought a larger and more permanent presence of allied forces on Nato’s eastern flank since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Warsaw has argued that a stronger US military footprint would bolster deterrence and strengthen the alliance’s eastern defences.The prospect of a permanent US base had gained momentum earlier this year. Polish defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said in June that the US Department of Defense was receptive to Poland’s proposal to host a permanent American military presence, although he stressed that no final decision had been made at the time.Kosiniak-Kamysz made the comments after meeting US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in Brussels. During the same period, Hegseth announced a review of US troop deployments across Europe, potentially opening the door to changes in the American military footprint on the continent.The United States already has troops stationed in Poland, but they have so far been deployed on a rotational basis rather than as part of a permanent US base.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Husband and wife get trapped in premier hiking destination; only one of them makes it out alive
articles.summary: Trapped in deep snow at 7,000 feet in Washington's Enchantments on a hike with her husband, a woman succumbed to the elements as a storm blocked multiple helicopter rescue attempts.
articles.body: A sudden and powerful storm over Washington state's Cascade Mountains quickly turned a challenging hike into a fight for survival for an Oklahoma couple. The pair was navigating the rugged "core zone" of the remote Enchantments wilderness when they were engulfed by heavy, deep snow. By late afternoon, the freezing, high-elevation conditions brought their trek to a desperate halt. 2 MYSTERY DEATHS AT ZION NATIONAL PARK PROMPT URGENT QUESTIONS ABOUT VISITOR SAFETY At 5:26 p.m., the husband sent an urgent text to 911. He reported to dispatchers that their clothes were soaked through from the storm, and his wife was physically unable to continue moving, according to FOX 13 Seattle. Help could not reach them in time. The stranded hiker, identified as 45-year-old Sybil Claborn of Oklahoma City, succumbed to the extreme elements and died in the snow Sunday. Before the rescue team reached them, Claborn's husband tried to carry her out but was unable to do so. They were stranded at an elevation of roughly 7,000 to 8,000 feet, about 8 to 10 miles from the nearest trailheads. TEEN HIKER'S DISAPPEARANCE ENDS IN TRAGEDY AT NATIONAL PARK WITH KEY QUESTION REMAINING The situation prompted a frantic rescue effort involving multiple agencies, but the severe weather repeatedly thwarted attempts to reach the couple by air. The sheriff's office requested a hoist-equipped helicopter at 6:51 p.m., and an Army helicopter launched from Yakima shortly after 8 p.m. Stormy conditions forced the helicopter to turn back as the husband remained in contact with 911 and reported that Claborn's condition was deteriorating. A second Army helicopter attempt around 10:50 p.m. was also unsuccessful, while Chelan County Mountain Rescue crews continued toward the couple on foot. Her husband was warmed inside a tent before he was transported to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth for treatment. articles.title: Philadelphia home search uncovers possible human ashes, images of 7 missing women: police
articles.summary: Ashtrays containing possible human remains and images of seven missing women were found among over 1 million files inside Eugene Horsch's Philadelphia home.
articles.body: Philadelphia police found images of seven missing women, including two who appear unconscious and injured, while searching more than 1 million images recovered from a home where investigators also found five urns believed to contain human ashes, authorities said Wednesday. Initial analysis of the images showed two missing women — 27-year-old Gabrielle Armando and 26-year-old Maribel Fresses — lying unconscious in the Chew Avenue home with apparent injuries, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said during a news conference. Metadata from the images show they were taken in 2017. CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS "Both women remain missing and have not been seen," Vanore said. "To date, neither their bodies nor any DNA evidence have been recovered." The home belonged to deceased pornographer Raymond "R.C." Horsch and was occupied by his son, Eugene Horsch, whose June arrest sparked the investigation. On June 19, a Federal Park Ranger arrested Eugene Horsch, 44, after investigating him and a female passenger sitting in a BMW outside of Philadelphia's Independence Mall, Vanore explained. "During the course of that investigation, officers recovered two firearms, narcotics, and identification impersonating a federal law enforcement officer, and he was charged. Task force officers from the DEA were able to develop probable cause that same day and serve a warrant on Mr. Horsch's residence," Vanore said. The female passenger presented police with a false identification using the name Blair Tonzelli, a woman who has been missing since 2023, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to Fox News Digital. FOUL ODOR AT NYC SCHOOL LEADS POLICE TO BODY HIDDEN IN CHIMNEY The true identity of the woman in the vehicle has not been released. Tonzelli's whereabouts remain unknown. After obtaining a warrant, investigators found "a homemade laboratory of some kind in the basement area, five urns believed to contain human ashes and a large amount of digital evidence — including computers, hard drives, flash drives, DVRs, cameras and phones," Vanore said during the press conference. Investigators have identified 58 people in the videos and images they found in the home. articles.title: US judge orders Kennedy Center to give 30-day notice before major changes, including demolition
articles.summary: US News: A US federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to give 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including .
articles.body: A US federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to give 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition, after President Donald Trump warned that the deteriorating performing arts complex could be “ripped down”.US District Judge Christopher Cooper said the clarification was necessary “given more recent events”, including the center’s sudden closure to the public on Wednesday, reported AP.The Kennedy Center said the shutdown was prompted by safety concerns. Executive director and chief operating officer Matt Floca said there were “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration”.The center will remain closed for at least seven days while officials assess parts of the building that have suffered severe deterioration. The decision followed a Tuesday board vote to close the complex indefinitely for repairs after an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month.The closure has become part of a wider legal and political dispute over the Kennedy Center under Trump, who became its chairman last year after his allies took control of the board.Trump and Kennedy Center linkTrump has defended efforts to renovate the ageing building, saying Wednesday that without repairs, “it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape.”Congress has allocated $257 million for repairs, but Trump has said the work should proceed only alongside plans to add his name to the institution.The latest court action followed a case filed by Representative Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and Kennedy Center trustee, who challenged the sudden closure. Her lawyers argued that describing it as temporary was “a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently”.Cooper rejected a request for an emergency hearing but clarified that his order bars demolition or other major physical changes without 30 days’ notice.The judge had previously ruled that the center’s decision to add Trump’s name was unlawful and ordered it removed. The Trump-aligned board later voted again to put his name on the facade, along with proposals to rename the plaza and add further inscriptions. Cooper blocked those plans on Tuesday, saying they could not proceed “without Congress’s blessing”.The dispute has also drawn criticism from Barbra Streisand, a 2008 Kennedy Center honoree, who described the controversy as “galling and painful to witness”.Of Trump’s effort to add his name to the center, Streisand said she was angered at seeing the institution become the subject of a “bitter struggle over one man’s name and unchecked ego”.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target
articles.summary: An 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target has been backed by England's former national cancer director.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England.

An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target has been backed by Professor Sir Mike Richards, England's former national cancer director, and Baroness Louise Casey, who's leading a major review of adult social care.

In a report, Alzheimer's Society and the King's Trust said a "cancer-style revolution" was needed to improve dementia care, which they described as being "stuck in the 20th century".

In a speech at Alzheimer's Society conference on Thursday, Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report .

She said: "The report that the Alzheimer's Society published today on going on the journey that we've been on with cancer, with Alzheimer's and dementia, I think that's spot on."

The minister said dementia had been "neglected for far too long".

She added: "And nowhere is this division between health and social care felt more sharply than by people living with dementia in their families, too often left to navigate a shattered system at the most difficult time in their lives."

The government has committed to appointing a top official to oversee dementia care and publish a new plan - a modern service framework - to speed up support for those with the disease by the end of the year.

McGovern said the government would "appoint a dementia tsar, backed with real expertise".

Currently there is no waiting-time target for dementia in England.

In contrast, the NHS sets waiting-time targets for cancer diagnosis and treatment.

Professor Richards was the national cancer director when these cancer targets were introduced in 2000, and said he thought an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target for dementia patients was achievable.

He said setting such a target would require "political initiative" and extra funding.

"All of that is going to cost more money but remember the toll that this condition is taking at the moment, both on the people affected by dementia themselves and their relatives," the professor said.

The same proposal has been made by Baroness Casey.

In a letter to former Health Secretary Wes Streeting in March, she said the government should look at "how dementia can be put on a level playing field with other conditions, for example by setting national standards for dementia diagnosis, including an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target".

Speaking to the BBC, Baroness Casey said she agreed with the proposal to emulate cancer care.

She said: "I think the National Health Service and more generally all of us have stuck our heads in the sand about it, and it's time we started saying, yes, we should have a similar mission, and we should do as much as we possibly can on dementia, and now."

Baroness Casey is expected to publish her recommendations on social care reform next summer.

About one million people are living with dementia in the UK, a figure expected to reach 1.4 million by 2040.

Burnham cancelled his engagements earlier this week after the death of father, Roy, who had Alzheimer's disease.

Returning from compassionate leave, he said his father would have wanted him "back out there" to bring forward "the changes that he always pushed me to make".

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

Burnham has said he will wait for Baroness Casey's recommendations before deciding what changes to make to social care and how it's funded.

articles.title: In 2000, Bob Dylan sold his Harlem townhouse for $560,000; after a preservation-led renovation, the four-storey Strivers’ Row residence has now sold for $2.8 million
articles.summary: News News: The 1893 Renaissance Revival townhouse in Harlem’s historic Strivers’ Row, once home to Bob Dylan, has sold for $2.8 million after nearly a year on th.
articles.body: The 1893 Renaissance Revival townhouse in Harlem’s historic Strivers’ Row, once home to Bob Dylan, has sold for $2.8 million after nearly a year on the market, according to a report by 6sqft. The four-storey residence at 265 West 139th Street closed at a price below its asking price. Last summer, the sellers listed it on the market asking $3 million, then dropped the price to $2.75 million in January before finding a buyer.The well-preserved townhouse is on one of New York's most architecturally significant blocks. The 133-year-old structure is everything one would hope for in a historic residence.Bob Dylan’s homeThe Harlem townhouse was once owned by the legendary singer-songwriter Bob Dylan. The ‘Blowin’ in the Wind’ singer called this Manhattan residence home from 1986 until 2000, according to a report by the WSJ. The notoriously private artist maintained a low profile on Strivers' Row. He simply existed, like other residents on a block where privacy was part of the bargain.Originally built in 1893, the Harlem house was designed by the McKim, Mead & White firm. The four-storey, 4,500-square-foot home is every bit as impressive as its history. In 2000, he sold the townhouse for $560,000, according to 6sqft.New buyers and renovationsFor the next decade, it passed through hands and listings. In 2018, retired attorney Isam Salah and former editor-in-chief of Elle magazine Elaina Richardson bought it for $3.17 million. For the married couple, Dylan’s legacy wasn’t the major attraction. But they were certainly reminded of it by the groups of tourists and curious passers-by. “Do you know Bob Dylan used to live in your house?” people sometimes asked, Salah told the outlet. And the couple would simply acknowledge, “Yes, we know.”After buying the townhouse, the couple made some renovations. Radiant heating was threaded through 19th-century floors. The kitchen was upgraded with modern appliances, while the vestibule retained its original tilework. Bathrooms were outfitted with marble and high-end fixtures. They added soundproof windows while still preserving the original woodwork. The Palladian windows stayed intact, and the four-foot-tall safe was reused as a bar. Much of the renovation work is not immediately visible. And that was exactly their plan. They wanted modern features such as central HVAC, radiant heating, CitiQuiet windows and mesh Wi-Fi to make it possible to live comfortably while still maintaining the original character. The home's beautiful architectural features, such as mouldings, pocket doors and galleries, remained untouched. They also rebuilt the rear terrace. The carport and garage also got an upgrade. They upgraded the amenities and kept the exteriors unchanged.What the new buyer getsThe historic townhouse sold for $2.8 million. Though it's slightly below asking, it reflects the demand for such homes. The new owners not only inherit a piece of Harlem’s history but also a carefully restored home with modern comforts. The four-storey townhouse has five bedrooms. The parlour floor stretches more than 50 feet of connected living and dining space, with 10-foot ceilings. The restored kitchen has premium appliances and is connected via a butler's pantry to a dining area framed by a trio of Palladian windows that pulls northern light across the original hardwoods.The two bedrooms on the third floor share a marble bathroom with radiant heated floors. There are three more bedrooms on the top floor, one of which has a magnificent view of 139th Street. Below ground is a sealed cellar that works as a laundry space, workbench room and storage area. The rebuilt rear terrace is perfect for entertaining, while a private carport and garage are an almost unheard-of convenience in Manhattan, along the residents-only alley.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Russia’s plans may include strikes against Ukraine’s allies, Poland says
articles.summary: Warsaw also says it scrambled military planes in response to a Russian attack in western Ukraine, close to its border.
articles.body:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that intelligence information suggests Russia plans to launch drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine.

Warsaw’s leader outlined the assessment during an address to parliament on Thursday, saying that the attacks will be meant to weaken NATO’s ability to act collectively in response.

“According to intelligence assessments, Russia’s plan … includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” Tusk said.

European countries suspect Moscow of being behind a series of acts of sabotage in recent months to put pressure on the allies, especially Germany, helping Kyiv in its bid to resist Russia’s full-scale invasion – something the Kremlin has vigorously denied.

“These potential strikes would be quote-unquote ‘accidental’ in nature, intended to paralyse or at least weaken the resolve of NATO states to invoke the relevant NATO provisions in the event of aggression against a member country,” Tusk added.

He did not elaborate on which intelligence agencies had provided the warning.

He also said such attacks by Russia could coincide with “political changes in certain European countries granting power – or at least a powerful voice – to those who, increasingly invoking noble slogans of peace, pacifism and needless casualties, will call for peace – or rather, the total capitulation of Ukraine”.

Tusk appeared to be referring to the advance of more Russia-friendly parties such as Alternative for Germany (AfD) and National Rally in France.

Earlier on Thursday, Poland said it had scrambled military planes in response to a Russian attack in western Ukraine, close to the Polish border.

Airports in Rzeszow and Lublin were temporarily closed, and residents of two eastern regions of Poland received air raid warnings. Local media reported that sirens had sounded and that pupils in some schools had sought shelter.

“Very close to the Polish border, not far from Dorohusk, a petrol station was most likely attacked again,” Tusk said.

On Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train in Ukraine, just two kilometres (1.6 miles) from the Polish border.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said Poland was strengthening airspace protection.

“We have increased F-16 and helicopter activity, and are reinforcing our air defence and rapid response systems,” he wrote on X.

Tusk said he would visit Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday to discuss cooperation within the Integrated Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries developing an air defence system with Ukraine as a cheaper alternative to the US-built Patriot.

articles.title: Archbishop withdraws award from Muslim cleric who praised Bin Laden
articles.summary: The award was handed out last week, on the anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.
articles.body:
The Archbishop of Canterbury has withdrawn an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama Bin Laden.

Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi received the award for reconciliation and interfaith cooperation from Dame Sarah Mullally last week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

Lambeth Palace faced a backlash after it emerged Ashrafi praised Bin Laden - the architect of the 2001 attacks - as someone who had "been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British", in comments from 2007.

Ashrafi also reportedly said he would give Bin Laden the title Saifullah, which means "Sword of God". He told the BBC his remarks had been "totally taken out of context".

Lambeth Palace now says "comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led (us) to reconsider this award and we can now confirm that the award has been withdrawn".

In presenting the award last week, the Archbishop's office said Ashrafi was being honoured for "his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance".

His award was presented by Dame Sarah in a ceremony that coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US in which nearly 3,000 people were killed.

Ashrafi told the BBC that his remarks had been "totally taken out of context" and the backlash had been "an unfair campaign" against him.

He said that he was only speaking about Bin Laden in 2007 in response to "the hurt felt by many Muslims" over a knighthood being awarded to the Satanic Verses author Sir Salman Rushdie.

But he defended the comparison he made between an author and a man who was behind the deaths of thousands of people.

Criticism of Ashrafi has gone beyond his comments about Bin Laden.

In giving him his award for promoting interfaith harmony last week, Lambeth Palace had cited the fact that Ashrafi had intervened in the 2012 case of Rimsha Masih, a young Christian girl in Pakistan falsely accused of blasphemy.

But Ashrafi has otherwise been supportive of Pakistan's blasphemy laws that have led to an estimated 2000 people being prosecuted since the late 1980s.

They include a disproportionately high number of Pakistan's minority Christians and Ahmadis in particular, but many majority Sunni Muslims too.

Ashrafi claimed the blasphemy laws actually "save lives", stopping people taking matters into their own hands.

But Human Rights Watch said last year that "the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs".

The organisation has called on the Pakistani government to urgently reform the laws to prevent them "being weaponised to [...] attack marginalised communities".

articles.title: Girlfriend detained by ICE after OPT denial: Redditor says she had no criminal record, no prior removal order
articles.summary: US News: A Redditor claimed that his girlfriend, who was in the US on a valid F-1 visa, was detained by ICE in Atlanta after her OPT application was denied. Th.
articles.body: A Redditor claimed that his girlfriend, who was in the US on a valid F-1 visa, was detained by ICE in Atlanta after her OPT application was denied. The Redditor said the OPT application was denied because of an apparent error with dates, against which an appeal has already been filed, and she was given a 60-day grace period that would not have expired until October. "ICE agents approached her in a public place with an arrest warrant. From what I've heard, they questioned why she was still in the U.S. after her OPT denial. She has no criminal record and, to my knowledge, no prior removal order," the Redditor said."Her school informed her that her grace period had started following the denial. An immigration attorney subsequently filed a motion challenging the decision, but ICE detained her while the motion was still pending," the post said detailing the case"She is currently in custody, and we have not yet confirmed whether a removal order exists. I'm currently working on hiring an immigration attorney to handle her detention, but I would really appreciate hearing from anyone who has experienced a similar situation. Has anyone experienced ICE detention while an OPT motion was pending?" the Redditor asked.The nationality of the girlfriend was revealed to be Mexican.What happens after an OPT denial?An OPT denial does not automatically mean that the student has to leave the US that same day. The key issue is what happens to the student's underlying F-1 status and whether the student is still within an applicable grace period.Under the F-1 rules, students generally receive up to 60 days after completing their course of study and authorized practical training to prepare for departure or take other steps to maintain status. USCIS also recognizes this 60-day period in its guidance on unlawful presence.There is also specific SEVP guidance dealing with an OPT withdrawal or denial. It says that when OPT is withdrawn or denied, the OPT authorization ends and the 60-day grace period runs from the date of the withdrawal or denial. The guidance says the student must either leave the US when that grace period expires or take other steps to maintain status.Many social media users commented that the grace period is discretionary and can be revoked. "USCIS status decisions and ICE enforcement don't always move in sync. Grace period status isn't always reflected in real-time in the databases ICE checks, and having a pending motion to reopen/reconsider doesn't automatically stop enforcement action. 'No criminal record' doesn't help much here. If there's no final order, an immigration judge may be able to set bond. This is usually the fastest way to get someone out of physical detention while the case proceeds," one suggested.Why the case matters to international studentsThough there is no verified information about this particular case, the Reddit post t comes at a particularly sensitive time for international students in the US.OPT is one of the main routes through which F-1 graduates obtain temporary work authorization after completing their studies. The administration is cracking down on OPT abuse and many students may get OPT denied.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: This California city asks residents to map pollution, housing and park access through ‘Walk and Roll’ events for its first Environmental Justice plan
articles.summary: US News: Pasadena is developing its first Environmental Justice Element, bringing residents into the process of identifying environmental burdens and gaps in a.
articles.body: Pasadena is developing its first Environmental Justice Element, bringing residents into the process of identifying environmental burdens and gaps in access to services across the California city. As part of the initiative, the city is holding “Neighbourhood Walk and Roll” events alongside surveys, workshops and other outreach activities. Residents are being encouraged to share their experiences of neighbourhood conditions, while city staff examine pollution, housing, parks, mobility and other factors. The information will help shape policies and priorities in the proposed Environmental Justice Element.Pasadena’s ‘Walk and Roll’ programme puts neighbourhoods on the mapAccording to the Pasadena Planning & Community Development Department, the Neighborhood Walk and Roll events form part of Pasadena’s wider community engagement process for its first Environmental Justice Element. The city has scheduled walking and rolling tours as it works to define environmental justice communities during summer and autumn 2026. The programme is designed to combine data with residents’ experiences of their neighbourhoods. Pasadena is also using surveys, pop-up events, community discussions and youth activities to collect local input. Earlier activities included map-making sessions in which young people explored the different environmental and social layers used to identify community vulnerabilities.Pollution and housing are among the issues being examinedPasadena’s Environmental Justice Element covers several areas that can affect residents’ everyday surroundings. These include exposure to air pollution, contaminated water and hazardous materials, as well as access to safe, sanitary and affordable housing. The city says environmental justice concerns can arise when pollution-generating infrastructure or land uses are located close to homes. Its preliminary analysis combines pollution, socioeconomic and public-health information to identify areas that may experience multiple burdens. CalEnviroScreen, developed by the California Environmental Protection Agency, is one of the data sources being used.Park access and walking are part of the wider pictureThe initiative also looks beyond pollution and housing to examine whether residents can reach public facilities and enjoy opportunities for active living. Pasadena’s environmental justice topics include equitable access to parks, community facilities, libraries, public transport and city programmes. The city is also considering safe walking, cycling and recreation across neighbourhoods. This means the community engagement process is not limited to identifying environmental hazards. Residents can discuss how streets, public spaces, transport and recreational facilities affect daily life, giving planners information that may not be captured through environmental datasets alone.Pasadena is using community input to shape its first EJ elementThe city says community input will help refine its preliminary environmental justice boundaries and ensure they better reflect residents’ lived experiences. Its initial map identifies seven census tracts concentrated in northwest Pasadena, where available data indicates relatively high transportation-related air pollution, lead exposure and economic burdens. The boundaries are preliminary and can change as the engagement process develops. Pasadena’s current timeline places policy development in winter 2026 to spring 2027, followed by solutions and priorities in spring 2027. A draft Environmental Justice Element is planned for autumn-winter 2027, followed by commission and City Council hearings.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
